name: FM24CL16B-GTR
title: FM24CL16B: 16 Kbit (2K x 8) I2C serial F-RAM, 2.7 V to 3.65 V
summary: A 16 Kbit nonvolatile ferroelectric RAM organised as 2048 bytes, reached over a two-wire I2C bus at up to 1 MHz from a 2.7 V to 3.65 V supply. A byte is committed to the array as soon as its eighth bit arrives, so writes run at bus speed with no write delay and no polling. It is a hardware drop-in replacement for a serial I2C EEPROM; pins 1 to 3 are unconnected, the top three address bits travel in the slave address byte, and a WP pin locks the whole array. FM24CL16B-GTR is the 8-pin SOIC part on tape and reel, industrial range -40 °C to +85 °C; an 8-pin DFN version exists.

operation.text: 2,048 one-byte locations picked by an 11-bit address: an 8-bit row address chooses one of 256 rows and a 3-bit segment address one of 8 segments in the row. Access takes no time beyond the serial transfer, so there is no ready condition to poll for.
The only power management inside is a simple power-on reset; keeping VDD inside its specified limits is up to the system.

The FM24CL16B is always a slave; the master generates the clock for every operation. START is SDA falling while SCL is high and STOP is SDA rising while SCL is high. Every command opens with a START and should close with a STOP. A START at any time aborts the operation in progress and readies the part for a new one; a STOP during an operation also aborts it. Apart from START and STOP, SDA must stay still while SCL is high.
If VDD falls below its minimum during operation, send a START before the next operation.

After the eighth bit of any byte the transmitter frees SDA and the receiver pulls it low to acknowledge. SDA left high is a no-acknowledge and ends the operation; after a failed byte this lets the master address the part again and recover the last byte. When reading, the master must not acknowledge the last byte it wants, otherwise the memory goes on driving SDA during the clock in which the master is trying to send STOP or a fresh command.

The first byte after START: bits 7-4 are the device type 1010b, bits 3-1 (A2, A1, A0) are page-select bits naming which 256-byte block is addressed, and bit 0 is R/W (1 = read, 0 = write). All bytes go MSB first.

On a write the master follows the slave address with one word address byte, the low 8 bits, which join the 3 page-select bits to form the full 11-bit address held in an internal latch. A read sends no word address: it latches its 3 page-select bits and uses the low 8 bits already in the latch, so reads begin at the byte after the previous access. The latch steps up just before the acknowledge of every data byte and wraps from 7FFh to 000h. A single read or write may move any number of bytes.

Slave address with R/W = 0, the word address, then any number of data bytes, each acknowledged by the memory; the address wraps from 7FFh to 000h. The array cycle is shorter than one bus clock and a byte is stored after its eighth bit, before its acknowledge, so any read or write may follow at once and acknowledge polling always reports ready. There is no page buffer. To drop a byte without changing memory, send START or STOP before its eighth bit.
WP high (VDD) protects every address: data bytes written there get no acknowledge and the address counter does not step. WP low (VSS) turns protection off. WP has an internal pull-down.

The master sends the slave address with R/W = 1, whose 3 page-select bits choose the block. On the next clock the memory starts sending the byte at the current address, made of those 3 bits and the 8 bits in the latch. Each byte the master acknowledges is followed by the next, the address wrapping from 7FFh to 000h.

Four ways end a read correctly: no-acknowledge on the 9th clock and STOP on the 10th (preferred); no-acknowledge on the 9th and START on the 10th; STOP on the 9th; START on the 9th. Otherwise the memory is likely to keep driving data and contend with the master.

Send the slave address with R/W = 0 and the word address to load the latch, then a repeated START, which cancels the write, and the slave address with R/W = 1. From there it is a current address read.

Each access reads and restores a whole 64-bit row, so reads use endurance cycles as writes do; a new row starts at every 8-byte boundary, and putting busy data in different rows spreads the wear. At 3000 accesses per second to one row, 10^12 cycles take 10 years.
Wait at least tPU = 1 ms after VDD reaches its minimum before the first START. VDD may fall below its minimum right after the last STOP (tPD = 0). VDD must ramp no faster than 30 µs/V up and down.
SDA has a Schmitt-trigger input buffer; SCL and SDA have a 50 ns noise suppression time constant (tSP). WP has an internal pull-down of 40 kΩ below VIL that weakens to 1 MΩ above VIH.
Hardware drop-in for an 8-pin serial I2C EEPROM, and runs the 100 kHz and 400 kHz bus timings as well as 1 MHz.
